items.title: How tight is the share?
items.prose: A fair coin is tossed 10,000 times. Each toss scores 1 for heads and 0 for tails, with variance $\tfrac14$.
items.question: What is the sd of the share of heads?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the sd of one toss, 0.5, by $\sqrt{10000}$.

byKey.var: That is the variance of the share. Take its square root.
byKey.count: That is the sd of the number of heads, $0.5\sqrt{10000}$. The share divides it by 10,000.
byKey.over-n: You divided the sd by $n$. The share's sd shrinks with $\sqrt n$.

explain.text: The share has sd $\sigma/\sqrt n = 0.5/100 = 0.005$. The count of heads has sd 50, which grows with $n$. One settles, the other wanders.

items.title: A model-free limit
items.prose: A fund's daily returns have mean 0.05% and sd 1.2%. Nothing else is known about their shape.
items.question: What is Chebyshev's bound on the chance a day's return is 3.6% or more from its mean?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn 3.6% into a number of sds, then use $1/k^2$.

byKey.normal: That is the normal answer. Chebyshev assumes no shape.

explain.text: A move of 3.6% is $k = 3$ sds, so Chebyshev caps its chance at $\tfrac19 \approx 0.111$. A normal model would say 0.0027.

items.title: The better bound
items.question: What is the smaller of Markov's and Chebyshev's bounds on $P(X \ge 20)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both bounds and keep the smaller.

byKey.markov: That is Markov's bound. Chebyshev uses the sd too and does better.
byKey.k: You used $1/k$ with $k = 5$. The bound is $1/k^2 = 0.04$.

explain.text: Here 20 is $k = 5$ sds above the mean, so $P(X \ge 20) \le P(|X - 10| \ge 10) \le \tfrac{1}{25} = 0.04$. Markov ignores the sd and gives only 0.5. More information gives a tighter bound.

items.title: A month of trades
items.prose: A desk makes 36 independent trades. Each has expected P&L £20 and sd £150. Use $\Phi(-0.8) = 0.2119$.
items.question: Approximately, what is the chance the 36 trades lose money in total?

feedback.correct: Zero is 0.8 sds below the mean of £720.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the total's mean and sd, then standardise 0.

byKey.one: That is one trade, $\Phi(-20/150)$, or an sd scaled by 36 rather than 6. Variances add, so the sd grows by $\sqrt{36}$.
byKey.no-scale: You kept one trade's sd of £150 for the total. Variances add, so the sd grows by $\sqrt{36} = 6$.
byKey.upper: That is the chance of a profit. Take the lower tail.

explain.text: The total has mean $36 \times 20 = 720$ pounds and sd $150\sqrt{36} = 900$ pounds. By the central limit theorem it is close to normal, so $P(\text{loss}) \approx \Phi(-0.8) = 0.21$.

items.title: Days until two standard errors
items.prose: A strategy truly earns 0.1% a day with daily sd 1.5%.
items.question: How many days until its true mean is two standard errors from zero?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $2\sigma/\sqrt n = \mu$ for $n$.

byKey.one-se: That puts the mean one standard error from zero. Use two.
byKey.no-two: You dropped the 2 and the square.

explain.text: $2 \times 1.5/\sqrt n = 0.1$ gives $\sqrt n = 30$, so $n = 900$ days, about 3.6 years.

items.title: Fifty backtests
items.prose: An analyst backtests 50 independent strategies with no skill. Each $t$-ratio is close to $N(0, 1)$. Use $1 - \Phi(2) = 0.0228$.
items.question: How many strategies do you expect to show $t > 2$ by luck?

feedback.correct: About one strategy in 50 looks good by luck.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of tests by the chance each passes.

byKey.both: That counts both tails. Only $t > 2$ looks like a positive edge.
byKey.zero: With no skill, flukes still happen: each test has chance 0.0228.

explain.text: Each test passes with chance 0.0228, so the expected count is $50 \times 0.0228 = 1.14$. The chance at least one passes is about 0.68. A single good backtest out of 50 is what luck predicts.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start the area at the left edge of bar 25.

byKey.nocc: That starts at 25, without the correction.
byKey.phi: That is the area below 24.5. Take the upper tail.

explain.text: The event $X \ge 25$ starts at 24.5, so $z \approx 1.30$ and the estimate is 0.0968. The exact value is 0.0978.

items.title: A window of outcomes
items.question: Estimate $P(18 \le X \le 22)$ with the continuity correction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Widen the window to 17.5 to 22.5, then standardise both ends.

byKey.nocc: That uses 18 to 22 without the correction, $z = \pm 0.63$. Widen to whole bars.
byKey.one-side: That is only the half from 20 to 22.5. Add the half from 17.5 to 20.

explain.text: Bars 18 to 22 cover 17.5 to 22.5, which is $z = \pm 2.5/3.162 = \pm 0.79$. The area is $2(0.7852) - 1 = 0.5704$, and the exact sum is 0.5704 too.

items.title: What the limit theorems promise
items.prose: Rolls of a fair die are independent. Let $S_n$ be the total of $n$ rolls.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: That gap typically grows like $\sqrt n$; only the average settles.

options.text: $(S_n - 3.5n)/\sqrt{n}$ is close to a normal for large $n$
Single rolls become normal once $n$ is large
options.why: A single roll is uniform on 1 to 6, however many you make.

feedback.correct: The average settles and the rescaled gap is normal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the average, the raw gap and the rescaled gap.

explain.text: Dividing the gap by $n$ gives the law of large numbers. Dividing by $\sqrt n$ gives the central limit theorem. Not dividing at all leaves something that wanders.
